citeAs: Bisk, Y., Zellers, R., Le Bras, R., Gao, J., and Choi, Y. (2020). PIQA: Reasoning about Physical Commonsense in Natural Language. AAAI.
creator: Yonatan Bisk, Rowan Zellers, Ronan Le Bras, Jianfeng Gao, Yejin Choi (Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence; Microsoft Research AI; Carnegie Mellon University; Paul G. Allen School for Computer Science and Engineering, University of Washington)
description: PIQA (Physical Interaction: Question Answering) is a benchmark dataset for physical commonsense reasoning in natural language. Given a goal and two possible solutions, exactly one of which is correct, models must choose the more sensible solution for accomplishing the physical task.
name: PIQA
rai:annotatorDemographics: Annotators were selected through qualification HITs; those participating in human evaluation achieved at least 90% on the qualification HIT. The paper also reports annotator pay averaged more than $15/hour according to self-reporting on turkerview.com and timing calculations.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The paper reports validation by other annotators, removal of low-agreement examples, majority-vote human evaluation, and vocabulary/length analyses to compare correct versus incorrect solutions. It also uses AFLite to reduce annotation artifacts and spurious stylistic biases.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators were shown instructables for inspiration and asked to produce three components: a physical goal, a valid solution, and a 'trick' solution that sounded reasonable but was wrong, often via a subtle semantic permutation. Qualification HITs were used before the main task, validation HITs were run afterward, a diff button highlighted differences between solutions, and low-agreement examples were removed.
rai:dataBiases: The paper explicitly discusses reporting bias in physical commonsense text and notes that unconstrained prompts led annotators toward prototypical kitchen and garage tools. To mitigate this, annotators were seeded with instructables to encourage atypical materials and object diversity, and AFLite was applied to reduce annotation artifacts and spurious biases.
rai:dataCollection: The dataset was collected through crowdsourced annotation using how-to instructions from instructables.com as inspiration. Annotators were prompted with links to instructables and asked to write a physical goal, a valid solution, and an invalid but plausible perturbation ('trick'), with data collected in batches and then validated by other annotators.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Source material came from instructables.com, a crowdsourced collection of how-to instructions for building, crafting, baking, repairing, and manipulating objects using everyday materials, often accompanied by images or videos and lists of required tools.
rai:dataCollectionType: User-generated content data, Manual Human Curator
rai:dataLimitations: The paper notes that some removed examples required expert-level domain knowledge and thus fell outside commonsense. It also states that some model 'mistakes' were actually correct but required a web search to verify, and emphasizes that the benchmark focuses on language-based physical commonsense rather than true interaction with the world.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Annotators created invalid solution variants by semantically perturbing their own valid solutions so that they remained syntactically and topically similar but became physically incorrect. The dataset was further filtered with AFLite, and examples were seeded from six instructables categories to encourage diversity.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The dataset was cleaned using AFLite to remove stylistic artifacts and trivial examples. Examples with low annotator agreement were removed during validation, train/development/test folds were automatically produced by AFLite, and the paper reports tokenization with spaCy and GPT BPE for analysis.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for benchmarking and analyzing physical commonsense understanding in natural language models, probing what pretrained models know about everyday physical interactions, and supporting progress toward language tools useful for robotics-language applications.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: AFLite for adversarial filtering and bias reduction; spaCy tokenization for analysis; GPT BPE tokenizer for length analysis.
